#RLab: Data Structures - Data Frames

#Part A — Creating Data Frames

#Question #1
```{r}
# Part a: check that all six vectors have the same length
Respondent <- c(1:20)
Sex <- c(2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 2)
FathersOccupation <- c(1, 3, 3, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3, 3, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1)
PersonsAtHome <- c(5, 7, 3, 8, 5, 9, 6, 7, 8, 4, 7, 5, 4, 7, 8, 8, 3, 11, 7, 6)
SiblingsAtSchool <- c(6, 4, 4, 1, 2, 1, 5, 3, 1, 2, 3, 2, 5, 5, 2, 1, 2, 5, 3, 2)
TypesOfHouses <- c(1, 2, 3, 1, 1, 3, 3, 1, 2, 3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2)

c(length(Respondent), length(Sex), length(FathersOccupation),
  length(PersonsAtHome), length(SiblingsAtSchool), length(TypesOfHouses))
```

```{r}
# Combine all six into a data frame
survey <- data.frame(Respondent = Respondent,
                     Sex = Sex,
                     FathersOccupation = FathersOccupation,
                     PersonsAtHome = PersonsAtHome,
                     SiblingsAtSchool = SiblingsAtSchool,
                     TypesOfHouses = TypesOfHouses)
print(survey)
```

```{r}
# Part a: structure and summary
str(survey)
summary(survey)
```

```{r}
# Part b: dimensions
dim(survey)
nrow(survey)
ncol(survey)
```

```{r}
# Part c: factors (stored in separate objects so survey stays numeric)
sex_f <- factor(survey$Sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female"))
father_f <- factor(survey$FathersOccupation, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                   labels = c("Farmer", "Driver", "Others"))
house_f <- factor(survey$TypesOfHouses, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                  labels = c("Wood", "Semi-Concrete", "Concrete"))

table(sex_f)
table(father_f)
table(house_f)
```

```{r}
# Part d: mean of all columns
colMeans(survey)
```

```{r}
# Part e: first five rows, all columns
survey[1:5, ]
```

```{r}
# Part f: select TypesOfHouses and store it as types_houses
types_houses <- survey$TypesOfHouses
types_houses
```

```{r}
# Part g: male respondents whose father was a farmer
survey[survey$Sex == 1 & survey$FathersOccupation == 1, ]
```

```{r}
# Part h: female respondents with 5 or more siblings in school
survey[survey$Sex == 2 & survey$SiblingsAtSchool >= 5, ]
```

#Question #2
```{r}
# Answer: Every row is one respondent, so every column has to have an answer
# for the same 20 people. If one vector is shorter, the answers would shift
# and get matched to the wrong respondent. data.frame() would also give an
# error about differing number of rows.
```

#Question #3
```{r}
# Answer: Sex, FathersOccupation, and TypesOfHouses are categories (nominal
# data), because the numbers are just codes. PersonsAtHome and SiblingsAtSchool
# are real counts. Respondent is only an ID number. Averaging Sex would be
# misleading because 1 and 2 are not amounts, so a mean of 1.85 does not mean
# anything.
```

#Question #4
```{r}
survey[survey$Sex == 1, ]

# Answer: The output only shows rows with a 1 in Sex. Someone who has not seen
# the legend would not know that 1 means Male, so they could think it means
# Female or something else. This shows that coded data is hard to read until
# it is labeled, and it is easy to misread it.
```

#Question #5
```{r}
nrow(survey[survey$Sex == 1, ])
sum(survey$Sex == 1)

# Answer: There are 3 males out of 20 respondents. This sample is small and
# has very few males, so I would not be confident generalizing any pattern to
# a larger population. A pattern from only 3 people could easily be random.
```

#Question #6
```{r}
summary(survey)

# Answer: R does not know the columns are categories because they are stored
# as plain numbers, so it treats them like any other numeric column. The
# meaning of the numbers only comes from the legend, which R does not have.
# So how data is stored (numeric) is different from what it means
# (categories). To fix this, I need to turn them into factors.
```

#Question #7
```{r}
mean(survey$PersonsAtHome)
mean(survey$Sex)

# Answer: The mean of PersonsAtHome (6.4) is meaningful because it is a real
# count, so it means the average household has about 6 persons. The mean of
# Sex (1.85) is not meaningful because Sex is a category. It only shows that
# most respondents are coded 2, which is better shown with a count or table.
```
